books.section: Topic 1.3 European exploration in the Americas
The Early Colonial Era: Spain Colonizes the New World

primary_sources: Bartolome de las Casas, A Short Account of the Destruction of the Indies (1542); German edition (1665)

options.text: Las Casas wrote his account to help Spain's rivals discredit the Spanish crown
options.misconception: Reverses Las Casas's purpose; he wrote to the Spanish crown, not to its rivals.

options.text: The same text served different purposes for different audiences over time
Protestant printers in northern Europe agreed with Las Casas's call for reform
options.misconception: Confuses use with agreement; printers used the account as propaganda whether or not they shared its reform goal.

options.text: Las Casas's account was read the same way by every audience that used it
options.misconception: Ignores the history; the crown read it as a reform plea and rivals read it as propaganda.

rationales.general:
1. Hear the first audience. Las Casas wrote to the Spanish crown to stop cruelty, not to help its rivals.
2. Hear the second audience. A century later, Protestant publishers in northern Europe used his account to discredit Spain.
3. Ask what changed between the two uses. A century passed, and the audience changed from the crown to Spain's rivals.
4. Put it together. The words stayed the same; the purpose changed with the reader.
Remember: a source's meaning depends on who uses it and why.
rationales.B: Las Casas wrote to reform Spanish rule, and a century later Protestant printers used his words to attack Spain. One text, two purposes, two audiences.
rationales.A: Las Casas wrote to the Spanish crown to stop the cruelty he described. Helping Spain's rivals was never his purpose.
rationales.C: Using an account as propaganda is not the same as agreeing with it. The printers used his words to discredit Spain.
rationales.D: The crown read the account as a plea for reform, while Protestant printers used it as propaganda. One text was read two different ways.

stem: Las Casas wrote his account to persuade the Spanish crown to stop the cruelty he described, yet a century later his words and images circulated in Protestant northern Europe as anti-Spanish propaganda. Which claim about the use of Las Casas's account is best supported by this history?

stimulus.source_note: Title page of a 1665 German edition of Bartolome de las Casas, public domain (Wikimedia Commons).
stimulus.text: Title page of a 1665 German edition of Bartolome de las Casas's writings about Spanish actions in the Americas. The title page is in German, the book was printed in northern Europe, and the scenes around the title show Spanish soldiers attacking Indigenous people and forcing them to carry goods. Las Casas wrote his account in Spanish in 1542.
